hook: One country sits on vast oil fields, its neighbor has none. Iceland heats its homes with water from hot rock, while a desert nation covers its land with sun-powered panels. Energy resources are not spread evenly: where they are depends on ancient geology and today's climate, and that shapes what every country burns, buys and builds.

figure.caption: Each region's geology and climate decide which energy resources it has.

chain.cause: Ancient swamps and seas buried organic matter in some basins
chain.effect: coal, oil and natural gas are concentrated in those sedimentary rocks

chain.cause: Plate boundaries bring hot rock near the surface
chain.effect: heat from underground is practical in places like Iceland, but not everywhere

chain.cause: Latitude, clouds and land shape decide sunlight, wind and falling water
chain.effect: renewable resources also vary from place to place

chain.cause: A country lacks the resources it uses
chain.effect: it must import energy, so its supply and prices depend on other countries

ideas: Fossil fuels lie where ancient swamps and seas buried organic matter: a few regions hold most of the world's oil and gas, and a few countries most of the coal.
A proven reserve is the part of a deposit that is known and can be recovered profitably with today's technology; it rises with higher prices or new techniques, not only new discoveries.

Renewables depend on place too: sunlight is strongest in dry, clear, lower-latitude regions; wind on coasts, plains and offshore; falling water on steep rivers with steady flow; Earth's internal heat at plate boundaries.
Years a reserve lasts = reserve ÷ production per year, if production stays the same.

misconception.wrong: A country's proven reserves are all the oil it has, so the number can only go down.
misconception.right: Proven reserves count only the oil that is known and worth recovering now. They can rise when prices go up or technology improves, even with no new discovery.

summary: Energy resources are spread unevenly because they depend on geology and climate. Fossil fuels sit in sedimentary basins where ancient organisms were buried; Earth's internal heat is near the surface at plate boundaries; sunlight, wind and falling water vary with latitude, clouds and terrain. A country without the resources it uses must import energy. Proven reserves count what can be recovered profitably now, and reserve ÷ yearly production estimates how long they last.
